title: I Was On Good Morning America Today
subtitle: And it wasn't the most validating experience of this morning.
body_html:
I doubt my regular readers are also regular Good Morning America viewers. For one thing, my articles do better when published early in the day. Unless you like reading humor-adjacent healthcare writing and learning about viral cheesecake stories at the same time, these seem like either/or life choices.

But at 8:40am EST today, I air on Good Morning America—”GMA” to its fans.

It was glorious…and also brief.

More importantly, my awesome patient, Gabrielle, tells her story of recovery from depression with BrainsWay SWIFT dTMS.

It’s still shocking to me

1. How awesome my patients are, routinely

2. How much better accelerated dTMS works for many, and

3. How insurance carriers—including hers—don’t cover this treatment.

I was an investigator on the trial—the one with 78% remission of depression with just 6 half-days of acute treatment. I think it’s fair to say, as a human who co-authored the first case report on one-day remission with accelerated dTMS (2019), then the first large scale case series, I have been a relentless nagging force to bring this treatment into the world.

How did my patient access this care absent insurance coverage? We just didn't get paid. I couldn’t stand to see her suffer after she switched from a plan that did cover her care…to one that didn’t. I’m not going to call out her carrier here, but I’ll forward them the clip for sure. You should do the same for your insurance. South Carolina Blues are already all over it.

We also have new data, after the GMA content was filmed. Not only is accelerated dTMS with SWIFT effective in the near term, it’s durable in the long term over 1 year:

Interim results included data of 64 patients. Response (remission) rates based on HDRS-21 at the four time points in the ACC-iTBS group ranged between 82%-100%(79%-100%), and in the SOC-HF group between 79%-94% (68%-80%). Response (remission) rates based on MADRS at the four time points in the ACC-iTBS group ranged between 86%-100% (67%-86%), and in the SOC-HF group between 82%-94% (70%-92%). …The quality-of-life data showed that in both groups 61-86% of the patients were in the normal range, while less than 21% had severe rate at any timepoint.

These durability data are best-in-class. It’s not apples-to-apples. The SNT long term follow up data (in a much more refractory cohort) required personalized re-treatment to maintain durability in many. My personal hunch is the much more refractory nature of the SNT sample is what matters here, but time will tell.

The national attention to this treatment option is good. Thanks, friends and coauthors at Brainsway, Magnus, Ampa, and others as we push accelerated TMS (and dTMS) protocols into the mainstream.

If you want to get accelerated treatment for your depression, reach out to us at Radial.

But this morning offered me another breaking story and that made me feel even more seen…

Inflammation and Depression.

For years I've been nagging everyone who will listen to me about the fact that I keep seeing people coming into my office, as a Psychiatrist and I keep making presumptive diagnoses of autoimmune conditions, referring patients to rheumatology, and having these diagnoses confirmed. Psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, non-radiographic ankylosing spondylitis, rheumatoid arthritis, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Sjögren's syndrome. You name it, I've made a presumptive diagnosis and had it confirmed. I've gotten a case wrong—Parkinson's Disease the source of rigidity on exam—out of 72 total referrals to rheumatologists.

I'm honestly insufferable about it.

I felt like I was on something, but there was pretty limited data. That has changed on notch today.

Interleukin 6 as a Treatment Target for Depression. A Proof-of-Concept Randomized Clinical Trial

Was published in JAMA psychiatry on May 20th.

The question they were asking was:

Can systemic interleukin 6 (IL-6) inhibition with tocilizumab improve depressive symptoms in patients with difficult-to-treat depression and low-grade inflammation?

Interleukins are immune molecules released by white blood cells:

Interleukins (ILs) are a large family of cytokines that function as key mediators of immune cell communication, regulating cell proliferation, differentiation, motility, and survival across both innate and adaptive immunity.[1] The term interleukin was first introduced in the late 1970s to describe leukocyte-derived cytokines, with IL-1 identified as a leukocytic pyrogen and IL-2 as a T-cell growth factor. Since then, more than 60 cytokines have been designated as interleukins, and to date, at least 38 have been formally recognized (IL-1 through IL-38).[2]

Leuk- a.k.a. white. “Cyte” a.k.a. cell White cell. Leukocyte. Communicated between white cells? Inter-leukin. White cell communicator molecules.

Ok, back to the paper. They enrolled subjects with “difficult-to-treat” Depression. Like all papers now, the supplemental materials are required to know what the heck is actually going on in the paper.

This was defined as:

Taking an antidepressant at an adequate dose (according to the BNF) for ≥4 weeks at eligibility assessment.

…and still having some depression:

Meet ICD-10 criteria for diagnosis of depression at eligibility assessment.

And, given it’s a tiny pilot of 30 people, none of the endpoints hit statistical significance. However, there was signal:

At the final follow-up, remission (7 participants [53.9%] vs 5 participants [31.3%]; number needed to treat [NNT] = 5) and response (6 participants [46.2%] vs 3 participants [18.8%]; NNT = 4) rates favored tocilizumab compared with placebo. Baseline hs-CRP level, but not IL-6 level, tracked depression improvement, suggesting hs-CRP may better predict immunotherapy response in depression than drug-specific biomarkers. Tocilizumab was well tolerated, with no serious adverse events or withdrawals.

So there you have it—I may be on to not only one thing, but two for depression.

Keep watching this space, people.
